title: The climate crisis is upon us—so why are deniers still getting airtime?
gist: Prompted by a hailstorm-wrecked hire car and public backlash to linking it (and Nepal's catastrophic floods) to climate change, Alan Rusbridger argues insurers like Munich Re are the most credible evidence for climate change because they are financially exposed, while legacy outlets like the Spectator keep platforming non-expert deniers such as James Delingpole and Matt Ridley.

themes.theme: Insurers as the real climate-risk signal

insights.claim: Reinsurance giant Munich Re is explicit in linking the increasing pattern of storms, flooding and wildfire to its mounting payouts, making major insurers' own risk pricing and claims data a more credible real-world signal of climate change than public commentary from pundits.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Track reinsurance repricing and payout trends (e.g. Munich Re disclosures) as a leading, financially-grounded indicator of physical climate risk, rather than relying on media debate over any single weather event.
insights.quote: Munich Re, one of the largest reinsurance businesses, is quite explicit in linking the increasing pattern of storms, flooding and wildfire with mounting payouts.

insights.claim: Nepal's Trishuli River rose by as much as 27 feet in just half an hour following a glacier collapse blamed in part on climate change, causing catastrophic flooding.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A concrete, extreme-magnitude data point on glacier-collapse flood risk relevant to physical climate-risk modeling in Himalayan river basins and any exposed infrastructure or insurance underwriting there.
insights.quote: the massive glacier collapse that caused the water levels on the Trishuli River to rise by as much as 27 feet in just half an hour

insights.claim: This century has recorded its five warmest summers since records began, a data point the author says is broadly accepted even by those who resist linking specific extreme-weather events to climate change.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A baseline scientific data point underpinning the broader climate-risk repricing thesis across insurance, agriculture, and infrastructure sectors.
insights.quote: the overwhelming scientific consensus that links climate change with this century's five warmest summers since records began
insights.locator: Same story with the warmest summer on record

themes.theme: Legacy media still platforms non-expert climate deniers

insights.claim: The Spectator, under editor Michael Gove, gave 1,100 words to TV critic James Delingpole and 1,000 words to Matt Ridley to dismiss any climate-change link to the Nepal floods, despite neither having relevant scientific expertise — Delingpole holds a BA in English literature and Ridley's doctorate concerned the mating systems of the common pheasant.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Illustrates a persistent editorial pattern at a specific, named UK outlet of platforming non-expert climate contrarians without rebuttal, a factor to weigh when assessing that outlet's coverage of climate and ESG-adjacent topics.
insights.quote: a fortnight ago he was given 1,100 words by Michael Gove to pronounce that we should ignore the Met Office and the pattern of boiling hot summers
insights.locator: Talking of crazy, for many years the leading loony voice on climate

insights.claim: The author's thesis is that public backlash against merely suggesting a link between an individual extreme-weather event and climate change is disproportionate to the actual scientific ambiguity involved, suggesting the reaction is driven more by culture-war identity than by evidence.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A framework for interpreting online backlash to climate commentary: intensity of reaction is a poor proxy for the strength of the underlying scientific case.
insights.quote: it's strange that suggesting a link between any extreme weather events today and global warming should make people quite so foamingly cross
insights.locator: I agree there may or may not be a connection

themes.theme: Corporate finance vs. customer service (Avis case study)

insights.claim: Avis-Budget Group took nearly $12bn in revenue last year and paid CEO Brian Choi about $6m, yet its emergency helpline was unresponsive and its social-media team took roughly 11 hours to respond to a stranded customer during a crisis in Switzerland.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A concrete, named example of large-company customer-service failure despite strong revenue and executive pay, useful as a case study when assessing service-quality risk versus reported financial performance in the car-rental sector.
insights.quote: The Avis-Budget group ('we are a leading global provider of mobility solutions') took nearly $12bn in revenue last year and paid its CEO, Brian Choi, a chunky $6m.
insights.locator: When you're marooned by a motorway in a foreign country

insights.claim: Citing Michael Kinsley's 2007 analysis, the author notes Avis was bought, sold or reorganized 17 or 18 times since 1946, with each transaction generating fees for bankers and lawyers and bonuses for executives, without necessarily improving the underlying rental-car service — framed as evidence that repeated financial restructuring extracts fees rather than creates operational value.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A transferable model for evaluating any asset with a long history of repeated PE/ownership churn: frequent restructuring can be a red flag that value is being extracted by financiers rather than built operationally, worth checking against Avis's and peers' current ownership/deal history.
insights.quote: Modern capitalism has two parts. There's business, and there's finance. Business is renting you a car at the airport. Finance is something else.
insights.locator: Reading the corporate filings, I was reminded of a famous 2007 piece

insights.claim: Avis's own SEC filing mentions climate change only once, in its risk-factors section, and frames it primarily as a reputational risk from 'negative claims or publicity' rather than an operational or physical risk to its fleet or business model.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A specific disclosure gap worth noting when screening corporate climate-risk disclosures: a company can treat climate change as a PR/reputational liability in filings rather than engaging with physical or transition risk substantively.
insights.quote: The Avis SEC filing mentions climate change just once, in its 'risk' section. It appears to be much more concerned about reputational risk, particularly 'negative claims or publicity regarding our Company or our operations.'
insights.locator: The Avis SEC filing mentions climate change
